entries.title: Greeting
entries.answer:
Maayong adlaw! I'm Sugbo Guide, your Cebu travel helper.
Ask me about North Cebu (Bantayan, Malapascua, Camotes), South Cebu (Oslob, Moalboal, Kawasan, Osmeña Peak, Simala), the city, getting around, or local products and pasalubong.

entries.title: Best time to visit
questions: When is the best time to visit Cebu?
entries.answer:
Dry season, roughly December to May, is the easiest time to visit. March to May is hottest and best for beaches and island hopping.
June to November is the rainy and typhoon season. Trips still run, but ferries and boat tours get cancelled when a storm signal is raised.
Expect big crowds and higher prices during Sinulog (January), Holy Week, and Christmas.

entries.title: Typhoons and cancelled ferries
questions: Are ferries cancelled during a typhoon?
What if there is a storm signal?
entries.answer:
When PAGASA raises a Tropical Cyclone Wind Signal, the Philippine Coast Guard usually suspends sea trips for small boats and sometimes ferries.
Check PAGASA and the Coast Guard (PCG Central Visayas) pages before leaving for Bantayan, Malapascua, Camotes, or Sumilon.
Keep a buffer day before your flight if your itinerary includes an island.

entries.title: Airport to the city
questions: How do I get from the airport to Cebu City?
Is there a bus from Mactan airport?
entries.answer:
Mactan-Cebu International Airport (MCIA) is on Mactan Island, Lapu-Lapu City.
Options to the city:
- MyBus airport route to SM City Cebu and other stops. Cheapest, about PHP 50 to 100 (verify current fare).
- Yellow airport taxi or white metered taxi. Ask the driver to use the meter.
- Grab car. Pick up at the designated Grab area.
Travel time to Cebu City is 30 minutes to over an hour depending on traffic. Use the CCLEX bridge route for the south part of the city.

entries.title: Getting around Metro Cebu
questions: How do I get around Cebu City?
entries.answer:
- Jeepneys: cheapest. Route codes (like 01K, 04L, 13C) are on the side and front. Base fare is around PHP 13 to 15. Pass the fare forward and say "Lugar lang" to get off.
- Taxi: metered. Make sure the meter is on.
- Grab: car rides through the Grab app. Motorcycle taxis like Angkas and Move It also operate.
- MyBus: air-conditioned buses linking the airport, SM City, SM Seaside, and Il Corso.
Traffic is heavy from 7 to 9 am and 5 to 8 pm, so plan around it.

entries.title: North and South bus terminals
questions: Where do I take a bus to the province?
entries.answer:
- Cebu South Bus Terminal (N. Bacalso Ave., Cebu City): buses to Carcar, Simala/Sibonga, Argao, Dalaguete, Oslob, Moalboal, Badian, Santander.
- Cebu North Bus Terminal (near SM City Cebu, Mandaue side): buses to Danao, Bogo, Hagnaya (for Bantayan), Maya (for Malapascua).
Ceres is the main operator. Air-conditioned buses cost a bit more but are worth it for long trips. Last trips usually leave in the late afternoon, so check before planning a return.

entries.title: Money, ATMs, and cash
entries.answer:
The currency is the Philippine peso (PHP).
Cards and GCash work in malls, hotels, and big restaurants in the city. In provincial towns, islands, markets, and on boats, bring cash.
ATMs exist in Bantayan (Santa Fe and Bantayan town), Moalboal, and Oslob town proper, but they run out of cash on weekends and holidays. Withdraw in the city first.
Money changers in SM, Ayala, and Robinsons malls usually give better rates than the airport.

entries.title: SIM cards and internet
questions: Where can I buy a SIM card?
Is there mobile data in the islands?
entries.answer:
Buy a Globe, Smart, or DITO SIM at the airport or any mall. Bring your passport because SIM registration is required. Some carriers also sell eSIMs.
Signal is good in the city and town centers but weak on some beaches, mountain trails, and small islands. Download offline maps before you go.

entries.title: Safety and emergency numbers
entries.answer:
Cebu is generally friendly and safe for tourists. Use normal city precautions: watch your phone and bag in crowded places like Colon and Carbon Market, and use metered taxis or Grab at night.
Emergency hotline: 911 (nationwide).
Major hospitals in the city include Chong Hua, Cebu Doctors' University Hospital, Perpetual Succour, and Vicente Sotto Memorial Medical Center.
If you lose something on a ride, Grab trips can be traced in the app.

entries.title: Church dress code and etiquette
questions: Is there a dress code for churches?
Can I wear shorts in Simala?
entries.answer:
Churches and shrines, especially Simala Shrine and the Basilica del Santo Niño, expect modest clothing: no shorts, sleeveless tops, or short skirts. Simala lends wraps at the entrance if needed.
Keep quiet during Mass and ask before photographing people praying.
Filipinos value politeness. A smile and "Salamat" (thank you) go a long way.

entries.title: Useful Cebuano phrases
questions: What language do they speak in Cebu?
entries.answer:
People speak Cebuano (Bisaya). English is widely understood.
- Maayong buntag / hapon / gabii: Good morning / afternoon / evening
- Salamat: Thank you
- Pila ni?: How much is this?
- Asa ang ...?: Where is ...?
- Lugar lang: Please stop here (jeepney)
- Palihug: Please
- Lami!: Delicious!
- Wala ko kasabot: I don't understand

entries.title: Sinulog Festival
entries.answer:
Sinulog is Cebu City's biggest festival, honoring the Santo Niño. The grand parade is held on the third Sunday of January, with novena Masses and events through the weeks before.
Book hotels months ahead, expect road closures, and keep valuables close in the crowds.
Other big fiestas: Kadaugan sa Mactan (April, Lapu-Lapu City) and many town fiestas through the year.

entries.title: Sample 3-day itinerary
questions: I have 3 days in Cebu, where should I go?
entries.answer:
A popular 3-day plan:
- Day 1, City: Magellan's Cross, Basilica del Santo Niño, Fort San Pedro, Taoist Temple, Temple of Leah, sunset at Tops.
- Day 2, South loop: leave around 4 am for Oslob, then Tumalog Falls, then Kawasan Falls or canyoneering in Badian. Stay in Moalboal.
- Day 3, Moalboal: sardine run and turtles at Panagsama Beach, Pescador Island hopping, then back to the city.
If you prefer white sand and a slower pace, swap Days 2 and 3 for Bantayan Island in the north.

entries.title: Daily budget
questions: How much should I budget per day?
entries.answer:
Rough daily budgets per person (2026, verify locally):
- Backpacker: PHP 1,500 to 2,500 (hostel, buses, local food)
- Mid-range: PHP 3,500 to 6,000 (hotel, some private transport, tours)
- Comfort: PHP 8,000 and up (resorts, private van)
Add tour fees separately, like whale shark watching, canyoneering, and island hopping.

entries.title: What to eat in Cebu
questions: What food should I try in Cebu?
What is Cebu famous for food?
entries.answer:
Must-try Cebuano food:
- Lechon: Cebu roast pig, flavored inside so it needs no sauce.
- Puso: rice cooked in woven coconut leaves.
- Sutukil: choose fresh seafood, then have it grilled (sugba), in soup (tuwa), or raw in vinegar (kilaw).
- Ngohiong: Cebuano spring roll.
- Siomai sa Tisa and tuslob buwa (Pasil) for street food.
- Sikwate (thick hot chocolate) with puto maya for breakfast.
Ask me about pasalubong to bring home, too.

entries.title: Fallback
entries.answer: I'm not sure about that one yet. Try asking about a place (Oslob, Bantayan, Moalboal), a topic (ferries, budget, safety), or local products (dried mangoes, danggit, chicharon).

entries.title: Cebu City heritage sites
questions: What can I see in Cebu City?
entries.answer:
The heritage area downtown is walkable in half a day:
- Magellan's Cross and the Basilica Minore del Santo Niño, the oldest Catholic church in the country.
- Fort San Pedro, a Spanish-era fort by the port.
- Colon Street, the oldest street in the Philippines.
- Parian District: Yap-San Diego Ancestral House, Casa Gorordo Museum, Heritage of Cebu Monument.
Go in the morning to beat the heat, and dress modestly for the Basilica.

entries.title: Busay uplands: Temple of Leah, Tops, Sirao
questions: What is the Temple of Leah?
Where can I see the city view?
entries.answer:
The Busay and Sirao highlands are 30 to 45 minutes from Lahug:
- Temple of Leah: a Roman-style temple built as a love monument, with a good view.
- Sirao Flower Garden: celosia flower farm, sometimes called the Little Amsterdam of Cebu.
- Tops Lookout: best city view at sunset.
- Taoist Temple in Beverly Hills, Lahug.
Hire a taxi, Grab, or habal-habal for a half-day loop since jeepneys don't cover all stops.

entries.title: Mactan Island beaches and Lapu-Lapu Shrine
questions: What can I do in Mactan?
entries.answer:
- Mactan Shrine (Liberty Shrine): the Lapu-Lapu monument marking the 1521 battle.
- Beach resorts along Maribago and Punta Engaño. Many offer day passes.
- Island hopping to Nalusuan, Hilutungan, and Pandanon for snorkeling. Boats leave from Mactan, about half a day.
- Olango Island Wildlife Sanctuary for migratory birds (best around September to March).
- Guitar workshops in Abuno and Maribago, where Mactan's handmade guitars are made.

entries.title: North Cebu overview
questions: What are the places to visit in North Cebu?
entries.answer:
North Cebu is quieter, with white-sand islands and fresh seafood:
- Bantayan Island: powdery beaches, Kota Beach, Virgin Island, dried fish and eggs.
- Malapascua Island: thresher shark diving at dawn.
- Camotes Islands: Lake Danao, caves, and calm coves.
- Along the way: Danao, Sogod, Bogo City, San Remigio, and Medellin.
Buses leave from the Cebu North Bus Terminal. Plan at least two days for any island.

entries.title: Bantayan Island
questions: How do I get to Bantayan Island?
entries.answer:
Getting there: bus from Cebu North Bus Terminal to Hagnaya Port, San Remigio (about 3 to 4 hours), then ferry to Santa Fe (about 1 hour). Several ferry trips run daily until late afternoon.
What to do:
- Swim at Kota Beach, Sugar Beach, and Paradise Beach.
- Ogtong Cave pool in Santa Fe.
- Island hop to Virgin Island and Hilantagaan.
- Rent a motorbike and loop to Bantayan town and Madridejos (old church, Kota Park).
Buy dried fish and eggs before you leave. Holy Week is very crowded, so book early.

entries.title: Malapascua Island
questions: How do I get to Malapascua?
entries.answer:
Getting there: bus from Cebu North Bus Terminal to Maya Port, Daanbantayan (about 4 to 5 hours), then a boat to Malapascua (about 30 to 45 minutes).
Highlights:
- Thresher shark dives at Monad Shoal, at dawn. You need Open Water certification, and Advanced is recommended for the depth.
- Bounty Beach and Langob Beach for swimming.
- Day trip to Kalanggaman Island (Leyte side) with its long sandbar.
Bring cash and arrive at Maya port before mid-afternoon.

entries.title: Camotes Islands
questions: How do I go to Camotes?
What to see in Camotes Islands?
entries.answer:
Getting there: bus or van to Danao City Port (about 1 to 1.5 hours from the city), then ferry to Consuelo, Camotes (about 2 hours).
Highlights:
- Lake Danao, the guitar-shaped lake, with bamboo rafts.
- Timubo Cave and Bukilat Cave.
- Santiago Bay and Mangodlong beaches.
- Busay Falls.
Rent a motorbike or habal-habal with a driver for a day tour.

entries.title: Towns along the north road
questions: What stops are there on the way north?
entries.answer:
Good stops on a North Cebu road trip:
- Liloan: Liloan lighthouse and Titay's rosquillos.
- Danao City: port to Camotes, and a lively public market.
- Carmen and Catmon: mountain views and roadside fruit stands.
- Sogod and Borbon: quiet beach resorts.
- Bogo City: the main hub of the far north.
- San Remigio: resorts and Hagnaya Port to Bantayan.
Roadside stalls sell fresh fruit, puto, and budbud. Stopping to buy helps small farmers directly.

entries.title: South Cebu overview
questions: What are the places to visit in South Cebu?
entries.answer:
South Cebu packs the classic adventures:
- Oslob: whale sharks, Tumalog Falls, Sumilon Island.
- Badian: Kawasan Falls and canyoneering.
- Moalboal: sardine run, turtles, Pescador Island.
- Dalaguete and Badian: Osmeña Peak, the highest point in Cebu.
- Sibonga: Simala Shrine.
- Carcar, Argao, and Boljoon: heritage churches and food.
Buses leave from the Cebu South Bus Terminal. A loop takes 2 to 3 days.

entries.title: Oslob whale sharks
questions: How do I see the whale sharks in Oslob?
How much is Oslob whale shark watching?
entries.answer:
Getting there: bus from Cebu South Bus Terminal to Tan-awan, Oslob (about 3 to 4 hours). Leave by 4 or 5 am since viewing ends around noon.
Fees: roughly PHP 500 for locals and PHP 1,000 for foreigners for snorkeling (verify current rates).
Rules: keep your distance, no touching, no sunscreen in the water, no flash.
Note: the sharks are hand-fed, which marine biologists criticize because it changes their behavior. If you prefer wild encounters, consider Malapascua (thresher sharks) or Moalboal (turtles and sardines) instead.
Combine with Tumalog Falls and Sumilon Island the same day.

entries.title: Tumalog Falls and Sumilon Island
questions: How to go to Sumilon Island?
entries.answer:
- Tumalog Falls: a curtain-like waterfall about 10 minutes from the whale shark area. Take a habal-habal down the steep road.
- Sumilon Island: a marine sanctuary with a shifting sandbar, reached by boat from Bancogon, Oslob. Day trips are possible.
Both pair well with the morning whale shark visit.

entries.title: Kawasan Falls and canyoneering
questions: How do I go to Kawasan Falls?
entries.answer:
Kawasan Falls is in Matutinao, Badian, about 3 hours by bus from the South Bus Terminal.
Canyoneering usually starts in Alegria or upstream Badian and ends at Kawasan. It takes 3 to 5 hours of river trekking, swimming, and jumps (all jumps are optional).
Packages run roughly PHP 1,500 to 3,500 per person with guide, helmet, life vest, and transport (verify).
Bring aqua shoes, a waterproof phone pouch, and go with an accredited guide. Avoid it after heavy rain.

entries.title: Moalboal sardine run and Pescador
questions: Where can I see the sardine run?
entries.answer:
Getting there: bus from Cebu South Bus Terminal via Barili (about 3 hours).
Highlights:
- Sardine run: millions of sardines right off Panagsama Beach, reachable by snorkeling from shore.
- Sea turtles along the reef wall.
- Pescador Island: island hopping and diving.
- White Beach (Basdaku) for swimming.
Moalboal is a good base for Kawasan and has many dive shops and budget stays.

entries.title: Osmeña Peak
questions: How do I go to Osmeña Peak?
What is the highest mountain in Cebu?
entries.answer:
Osmeña Peak (about 1,000 meters) is the highest point in Cebu, in Mantalongon, Dalaguete.
Take a bus to Dalaguete, then a habal-habal up to the jump-off. The hike to the summit is only about 20 to 30 minutes.
Go for sunrise for the best view of the jagged hills. It gets cool up there, so bring a light jacket.
You can trek across to Kawasan Falls in Badian (about 3 to 4 hours downhill) with a guide.

entries.title: Simala Shrine
questions: How to go to Simala Shrine?
entries.answer:
The Monastery of the Holy Eucharist (Simala Shrine) in Lindogon, Sibonga is a castle-like church known for devotees' prayers and testimonies.
Getting there: bus from Cebu South Bus Terminal to the Simala junction in Sibonga, then a habal-habal or tricycle up (about 1.5 to 2 hours total).
Strict dress code: no shorts or sleeveless tops. Weekends are crowded.

entries.title: Carcar, Argao, and Boljoon heritage
entries.answer:
- Carcar City: heritage houses, St. Catherine of Alexandria Church, and the famous chicharon at the public market.
- Argao: Spanish-era church and plaza, torta, and hablon handwoven fabric.
- Dalaguete: the vegetable basket and summer capital of Cebu, gateway to Osmeña Peak.
- Boljoon: the Patrocinio de Maria church, one of the best-preserved in the country, with a museum.
- Alcoy: Tingko Beach. Samboan: Aguinid Falls.
These are easy stops on the way to or from Oslob.

entries.title: Crossing to Dumaguete or Bohol
questions: How do I go from Cebu to Dumaguete?
entries.answer:
- To Dumaguete: bus to Liloan Port, Santander (southern tip), then a short ferry to Sibulan, Negros Oriental (about 20 to 30 minutes).
- To Bohol: fast craft from Pier 1 in Cebu City to Tagbilaran (about 2 hours). Book OceanJet or SuperCat in advance on weekends.

entries.title: Cebu dried mangoes
questions: Where can I buy dried mangoes?
entries.answer:
Cebu dried mangoes: Sweet, chewy dried Carabao mango slices. Cebu's best-known pasalubong.
Origin: Made from Carabao mangoes processed in Metro Cebu.
Where to buy: Pasalubong centers, malls, the airport, and factory outlets in Mandaue.
Typical price: PHP 100 to 200 per 100 g pack (approximate, check with the seller).
Tip: Buy local brands from Cebu processors to support mango growers. Check the expiry date.

entries.title: Danggit and dried fish
entries.answer:
Danggit and dried fish: Sun-dried rabbitfish (danggit), plus dried squid (pusit) and other dried fish. Fried crispy for breakfast with rice and vinegar.
Origin: Coastal towns, especially Bantayan Island and Daanbantayan.
Where to buy: Taboan Market (Cebu City) has the widest selection. On Bantayan, buy straight from processors near the port.
Typical price: PHP 600 to 1,200 per kilo for danggit, depending on grade (approximate, check with the seller).
Tip: Ask for boneless or unsalted (lamayo-style) if you prefer. Ask the seller to vacuum-seal for flights.

entries.title: Bantayan eggs and poultry
questions: Where do eggs in Cebu come from?
entries.answer:
Bantayan eggs and poultry: Bantayan's poultry farms supply eggs to much of the Visayas. Look for salted eggs and fresh trays.
Origin: Bantayan Island, the egg basket of the Visayas.
Where to buy: Markets in Bantayan town and Santa Fe, and roadside stalls on the island.
Typical price: Local market prices per tray (approximate, check with the seller).
Tip: Good to buy for your stay. Fresh eggs travel poorly, so choose salted eggs if taking them home.

entries.title: Carcar chicharon
entries.answer:
Carcar chicharon: Crispy pork crackling, including the famous 'with laman' (with meat) and bituka (intestine) versions.
Origin: Carcar City, South Cebu.
Where to buy: Carcar Public Market near the rotunda. Also sold in pasalubong shops in the city.
Typical price: PHP 150 to 300 per pack (approximate, check with the seller).
Tip: Buy on the way back from the south so it stays crisp. Pair it with spiced vinegar.

entries.title: Cebu lechon
questions: Where is the best lechon in Cebu?
Can I bring lechon on the plane?
entries.answer:
Cebu lechon: Whole roast pig stuffed with lemongrass, garlic, and spices. Famous for crispy skin and flavor that needs no sauce.
Origin: Talisay City and Carcar City, South Cebu.
Where to buy: Lechon houses in Talisay and Carcar, and well-known shops in Cebu City. Order by the kilo or whole.
Typical price: PHP 800 to 1,000 per kilo; whole lechon from about PHP 7,000 (approximate, check with the seller).
Tip: Order a day ahead for a whole pig. Some shops vacuum-pack lechon for travel.

entries.title: Rosquillos
entries.answer:
Rosquillos: Crisp, flower-shaped cookies first made in Liloan, the original from Titay's.
Origin: Liloan, North Metro Cebu.
Where to buy: Titay's in Liloan and pasalubong shops across Metro Cebu.
Typical price: PHP 80 to 150 per pack (approximate, check with the seller).
Tip: Visit the original Titay's on the way north to Danao or Bantayan.

entries.title: Otap
entries.answer:
Otap: Flaky, oval puff pastry with sugar. A classic Cebu pasalubong that pairs well with coffee or sikwate.
Origin: Metro Cebu bakeries.
Where to buy: Pasalubong centers, supermarkets, and bakeries in Cebu City and Mandaue.
Typical price: PHP 80 to 150 per pack (approximate, check with the seller).
Tip: It crumbles easily, so pack it on top of your bag.

entries.title: Argao torta
questions: What can I buy in Argao?
entries.answer:
Argao torta: Soft, sweet cake traditionally made with tuba (coconut wine) and pork lard, baked in a mold.
Origin: Argao, South Cebu.
Where to buy: Argao public market and home bakeries along the highway.
Typical price: PHP 20 to 40 per piece (approximate, check with the seller).
Tip: Best eaten within a few days. Great with sikwate.

entries.title: Argao hablon
questions: What handicrafts are made in Cebu?
entries.answer:
Argao hablon: Handwoven fabric made on wooden looms by local weavers, turned into scarves, bags, and table runners.
Origin: Argao, South Cebu.
Where to buy: Weaving centers and shops in Argao.
Typical price: PHP 200 to 1,500 depending on the item (approximate, check with the seller).
Tip: Buying direct from weavers keeps the tradition alive. Ask for a weaving demonstration.

entries.title: Mantalongon highland vegetables
questions: Where do vegetables in Cebu come from?
Is there a farmers market in Cebu?
entries.answer:
Mantalongon highland vegetables: Cool-climate vegetables like cabbage, carrots, bell pepper, and lettuce grown in the Dalaguete highlands.
Origin: Mantalongon, Dalaguete, the vegetable basket of Cebu.
Where to buy: Mantalongon public market (busiest early morning) and roadside stalls on the way to Osmeña Peak.
Typical price: Farm-gate prices, usually cheaper than city markets (approximate, check with the seller).
Tip: Visit the Mantalongon market at dawn before hiking Osmeña Peak. Farmers sell directly here.

entries.title: Sirao celosia flowers
questions: Are there farm tours near Cebu City?
entries.answer:
Sirao celosia flowers: Flower farms growing celosia and other cut flowers, also open to visitors as photo gardens.
Origin: Sirao, Cebu City highlands.
Where to buy: Flower farms in Sirao and Busay.
Typical price: Entrance about PHP 100 to 150; flowers by the bundle (approximate, check with the seller).
Tip: Go early morning for cooler weather and better light.

entries.title: Mactan guitars
questions: Where can I buy a guitar in Cebu?
entries.answer:
Mactan guitars: Handcrafted guitars and ukuleles from family workshops using local and imported woods.
Origin: Abuno and Maribago, Lapu-Lapu City.
Where to buy: Workshops and showrooms in Abuno and Maribago, Mactan.
Typical price: Ukuleles from about PHP 1,500; guitars from about PHP 4,000 (approximate, check with the seller).
Tip: Ask for a workshop tour. Workshops can pack instruments for flights.

entries.title: Puso, masi, and budbud
entries.answer:
Puso, masi, and budbud: Puso is rice in woven coconut leaves. Masi is a sticky rice ball with peanut and sugar. Budbud is sticky rice wrapped in banana leaf.
Origin: Made across Cebu, sold in every town market.
Where to buy: Town public markets, carenderias, and roadside stalls.
Typical price: PHP 5 to 30 per piece (approximate, check with the seller).
Tip: Masi and budbud make cheap road-trip snacks. Buy from local vendors along the highways.

entries.title: Tablea and sikwate
entries.answer:
Tablea and sikwate: Pure ground cacao tablets (tablea) used to make sikwate, the thick Cebuano hot chocolate.
Origin: Made from cacao grown in Cebu and nearby Visayas uplands.
Where to buy: Public markets, Carbon Market, and pasalubong shops.
Typical price: PHP 100 to 250 per pack (approximate, check with the seller).
Tip: Ask for locally grown cacao to support small farmers. Breakfast of sikwate and puto maya is a Cebu classic.

entries.title: Guso and seaweed
entries.answer:
Guso and seaweed: Fresh seaweed (guso, lato) eaten as salad with vinegar and tomatoes. Seaweed farming supports many coastal families.
Origin: Coastal farms around Cebu and nearby islands.
Where to buy: Coastal town markets, Carbon Market, and seafood restaurants.
Typical price: PHP 20 to 60 per serving (approximate, check with the seller).
Tip: Eat it fresh at a sutukil place. It doesn't travel well.

entries.title: Corn and bugas mais
entries.answer:
Corn and bugas mais: Cebu has a strong corn tradition. Corn grits (bugas mais) are eaten like rice, and boiled corn is sold along the highways.
Origin: Upland and northern farming towns.
Where to buy: Town public markets and roadside stalls.
Typical price: Local market prices (approximate, check with the seller).
Tip: Try a meal with bugas mais at a local carenderia for a true Cebuano experience.

entries.title: Banana chips and fruit snacks
questions: What fruit snacks can I bring home?
entries.answer:
Banana chips and fruit snacks: Sweet, crunchy banana chips and other dried fruit snacks from local cooperatives.
Origin: Small processors across Cebu.
Where to buy: Pasalubong centers, supermarkets, and cooperative stores.
Typical price: PHP 50 to 150 per pack (approximate, check with the seller).
Tip: Look for cooperative or barangay-made labels to support local producers.

entries.title: Pasalubong guide
questions: What can I bring home from Cebu?
entries.answer:
Top pasalubong and local products from Cebu:
- Food: dried mangoes, danggit and dried squid, Carcar chicharon, otap, rosquillos, Argao torta, tablea.
- Fresh from farms: Mantalongon vegetables, Bantayan eggs, highway fruits.
- Crafts: Argao hablon weaving, Mactan guitars and ukuleles.
Where to shop: Taboan Market for dried fish, Carbon Market for produce, pasalubong centers in the city, and town markets on your route.
Buying directly in the towns helps the farmers and makers most. Tap a product in the Pasalubong tab for details.

entries.title: Carbon and Taboan markets
questions: What can I buy in Taboan?
entries.answer:
- Carbon Market (downtown Cebu City): the oldest and largest farmers' market, with fruits, vegetables, flowers, and native goods. The redeveloped section is cleaner and easier to walk.
- Taboan Market (near Pasil): the dried fish market, with danggit, pusit, and more.
Go in the morning, bring small bills, and keep your phone secure in crowds.

entries.title: Bringing food on flights
questions: Can I bring danggit on the plane?
entries.answer:
Dried goods (mangoes, danggit, chicharon, otap) are fine in checked baggage when sealed. Ask sellers to vacuum-seal dried fish so it doesn't smell.
Lechon is allowed if packed well. Many shops offer travel boxes.
For international flights, check your destination's customs rules. Many countries restrict meat, fresh produce, and eggs.

products.price_range: PHP 600 to 1,200 per kilo for danggit, depending on grade
products.tip: Ask for boneless or unsalted (lamayo-style) if you prefer. Ask the seller to vacuum-seal for flights.

products.name: Bantayan eggs and poultry
products.origin: Bantayan Island, the egg basket of the Visayas
products.description: Bantayan's poultry farms supply eggs to much of the Visayas. Look for salted eggs and fresh trays.
products.where_to_buy: Markets in Bantayan town and Santa Fe, and roadside stalls on the island.
products.tip: Good to buy for your stay. Fresh eggs travel poorly, so choose salted eggs if taking them home.

products.name: Carcar chicharon
products.description: Crispy pork crackling, including the famous 'with laman' (with meat) and bituka (intestine) versions.
products.where_to_buy: Carcar Public Market near the rotunda. Also sold in pasalubong shops in the city.
products.tip: Buy on the way back from the south so it stays crisp. Pair it with spiced vinegar.

products.name: Cebu lechon
products.origin: Talisay City and Carcar City, South Cebu
products.description: Whole roast pig stuffed with lemongrass, garlic, and spices. Famous for crispy skin and flavor that needs no sauce.
products.where_to_buy: Lechon houses in Talisay and Carcar, and well-known shops in Cebu City. Order by the kilo or whole.
products.price_range: PHP 800 to 1,000 per kilo; whole lechon from about PHP 7,000
products.tip: Order a day ahead for a whole pig. Some shops vacuum-pack lechon for travel.

products.name: Rosquillos
products.description: Crisp, flower-shaped cookies first made in Liloan, the original from Titay's.
products.where_to_buy: Titay's in Liloan and pasalubong shops across Metro Cebu.
products.tip: Visit the original Titay's on the way north to Danao or Bantayan.

products.name: Otap
products.description: Flaky, oval puff pastry with sugar. A classic Cebu pasalubong that pairs well with coffee or sikwate.
products.where_to_buy: Pasalubong centers, supermarkets, and bakeries in Cebu City and Mandaue.
products.tip: It crumbles easily, so pack it on top of your bag.

products.name: Argao torta
products.description: Soft, sweet cake traditionally made with tuba (coconut wine) and pork lard, baked in a mold.
products.where_to_buy: Argao public market and home bakeries along the highway.
products.tip: Best eaten within a few days. Great with sikwate.

products.name: Argao hablon
products.description: Handwoven fabric made on wooden looms by local weavers, turned into scarves, bags, and table runners.
products.where_to_buy: Weaving centers and shops in Argao.
products.price_range: PHP 200 to 1,500 depending on the item
products.tip: Buying direct from weavers keeps the tradition alive. Ask for a weaving demonstration.

products.name: Mantalongon highland vegetables
products.origin: Mantalongon, Dalaguete, the vegetable basket of Cebu
products.description: Cool-climate vegetables like cabbage, carrots, bell pepper, and lettuce grown in the Dalaguete highlands.
products.where_to_buy: Mantalongon public market (busiest early morning) and roadside stalls on the way to Osmeña Peak.
products.price_range: Farm-gate prices, usually cheaper than city markets
products.tip: Visit the Mantalongon market at dawn before hiking Osmeña Peak. Farmers sell directly here.

products.name: Sirao celosia flowers
products.description: Flower farms growing celosia and other cut flowers, also open to visitors as photo gardens.
products.where_to_buy: Flower farms in Sirao and Busay.
products.price_range: Entrance about PHP 100 to 150; flowers by the bundle
products.tip: Go early morning for cooler weather and better light.

products.name: Mactan guitars
products.description: Handcrafted guitars and ukuleles from family workshops using local and imported woods.
products.where_to_buy: Workshops and showrooms in Abuno and Maribago, Mactan.
products.price_range: Ukuleles from about PHP 1,500; guitars from about PHP 4,000
products.tip: Ask for a workshop tour. Workshops can pack instruments for flights.

products.name: Puso, masi, and budbud
products.origin: Made across Cebu, sold in every town market
products.description: Puso is rice in woven coconut leaves. Masi is a sticky rice ball with peanut and sugar. Budbud is sticky rice wrapped in banana leaf.
products.where_to_buy: Town public markets, carenderias, and roadside stalls.
products.tip: Masi and budbud make cheap road-trip snacks. Buy from local vendors along the highways.

products.name: Tablea and sikwate
products.origin: Made from cacao grown in Cebu and nearby Visayas uplands
products.description: Pure ground cacao tablets (tablea) used to make sikwate, the thick Cebuano hot chocolate.
products.where_to_buy: Public markets, Carbon Market, and pasalubong shops.
products.tip: Ask for locally grown cacao to support small farmers. Breakfast of sikwate and puto maya is a Cebu classic.

products.name: Guso and seaweed
products.origin: Coastal farms around Cebu and nearby islands
products.description: Fresh seaweed (guso, lato) eaten as salad with vinegar and tomatoes. Seaweed farming supports many coastal families.
products.where_to_buy: Coastal town markets, Carbon Market, and seafood restaurants.
products.tip: Eat it fresh at a sutukil place. It doesn't travel well.

products.name: Corn and bugas mais
products.description: Cebu has a strong corn tradition. Corn grits (bugas mais) are eaten like rice, and boiled corn is sold along the highways.
products.where_to_buy: Town public markets and roadside stalls.
products.tip: Try a meal with bugas mais at a local carenderia for a true Cebuano experience.

products.name: Banana chips and fruit snacks
products.description: Sweet, crunchy banana chips and other dried fruit snacks from local cooperatives.
products.where_to_buy: Pasalubong centers, supermarkets, and cooperative stores.
products.tip: Look for cooperative or barangay-made labels to support local producers.
